blocks.content: docker stop asks a container to shut down gracefully, giving its process a chance to clean up before force-killing it if it does not respond in time.

docker stop does not kill a container instantly. It first sends a SIGTERM signal, the standard "please shut down" request, then waits a grace period, 10 seconds by default, for the process to exit on its own.

blocks.alt: SIGTERM first, then a waiting period

blocks.content:
docker stop web              # waits up to 10 seconds
docker stop -t 30 web         # give it up to 30 seconds instead

code.content:
docker stop web              # waits up to 10 seconds
docker stop -t 30 web         # give it up to 30 seconds instead

codes.bash:
docker stop web              # waits up to 10 seconds
docker stop -t 30 web         # give it up to 30 seconds instead

blocks.content: 2. If It Does Not Exit in Time, SIGKILL
blocks.text: 2. If It Does Not Exit in Time, SIGKILL

blocks.content: If the grace period elapses and the process has not exited, Docker escalates to SIGKILL, an immediate, unignorable termination. This is the safety net that guarantees docker stop always eventually succeeds, even against a process that never handles signals at all.

blocks.alt: A hard SIGKILL is the fallback if grace period expires

blocks.content: An application that properly handles SIGTERM gets the chance to finish in-flight requests, close database connections, and flush any pending writes before exiting, a meaningfully cleaner shutdown than being killed mid-operation.

blocks.alt: Handling SIGTERM properly means a clean exit, not a forced one

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker stop is a graceful request (SIGTERM, then a grace period) with a forced fallback (SIGKILL), not an instant kill.
Applications that handle SIGTERM properly shut down cleanly, applications that ignore it just get killed once the grace period runs out.
